newsitem.title: UK: Britain's Major resists pressure for EMU debate.
newsitem.headline: Britain's Major resists pressure for EMU debate.

text.p: British Prime Minister John Major, anxious to prevent fresh divisions in his party over Europe, on Thursday resisted demands for a full debate on plans for the introduction of a single European currency.

Major, getting his campaign under way for an election that is less than six months away, refused to give way to calls for a debate on documents detailing how a European currency will be introduced and how countries that do not join will be treated.

But he was warned by Eurosceptic MPs in his ruling Conservative party who oppose any move towards European integration that they could withdraw support for the government unless he backed down. Conservative MP Tony Marlow told a television interviewer: "By not having a debate...the government is riding rough-shod over parliament, it is being contemptuous of democracy.

"And, in that case, why should it deserve support, let alone why should anybody hold its whip?" said Marlow, who two years ago briefly lost the Conservative "whip", or membership of the party group in parliament, for rebelling against Major on Europe.
Another Eurosceptic, former Treasury minister David Heathcoat-Amory, who quit the government earlier this year in protest at its European policy, also issued a veiled threat.
He told the BBC: "We all want to support the government but only if the government looks after our freedoms."
The warnings were seen as sabre-rattling rather than a threat of imminent action.

Major has a majority of only one seat in the House of Commons, and will probably lose that in a by-election next month, but is expected to battle on into next year with the support of Northern Irish MPs.
Labour, ahead in polls, immediately sensed a weak point it could exploit to try to end 17 years of Conservative rule.

"How can the prime minister actually be trusted with Britain's future in Europe when the matters of internal party management of the Conservative party...always take precedence over the interests of Britain," said Labour leader Tony Blair.
"If he's not afraid of the debate, then let him call one," taunted Blair during question time in the House of Commons.

Major, arguing the regulations were not finalised and would only affect those countries that decided to join a single currency, fought back, saying Labour would not stand up to Europe and would give way to pressure.
"We are prepared to be isolated where necessary, we do defend the British interest," said a defiant Major.
The demand for a full debate came a day after the government suffered an embarrassing defeat in a parliamentary committee where it was trying to force the regulations through.

Labour committee members joined with Conservative Eurosceptics to protest that the government was trying to "smuggle in" the documents by using a "backstairs" committee rather than allowing a full House of Commons debate.
Major's refusal to change his mind on Thursday showed he intended to ignore the committee defeat and ride out the storm.

But he is under increasing pressure after Labour's new pledge to hold a referendum before taking Britain into a single currency, with Conservatives worried at their election prospects demanding a tougher government line on Europe.
